 Whoever dreamed up changing the clocks so the sun would set earlier deserves a giant wedgie.
 OK, so I am actually not that lazy, and I looked up why daylight saving time exists. Like many of the world’s bad ideas from the last 100 years, it can trace its origins to World War I. But the idea stuck, and even though everyone hates it, we still turn our clocks back every year when daylight saving ends.
 It’s amazing that in a country so divided that we’re ready to throttle each other like siblings on a road trip, we have widespread public compliance with time regulation. Unlike the peaceful transfer of power, it is an American norm that seems unbreakable.
 What holds Americans together on this issue? Is it the knowledge that someone we dislike is also suffering? Is it that we’re simply too busy to do anything about it?
 Or is it something else? Magic?
 When the days get shorter, my family gets sadder. My late-evening walks with my son stop. A blanket of gray clouds covers the sky and never seems to leave. Summer, with its endless days, fireworks, holidays and vacations, feels like magic. Fall feels like watching the magic slowly fade away until there’s nothing left but darkness.
 We celebrated the end of daylight saving time by taking a trip to Savannah. The city feels strangely familiar to me, even though I’ve never spent much time there. I grew up in Mobile, Alabama, and spent several years living in Anniston. With its port and midcentury neighborhood designs, Savannah feels very much like a cross between the two.
 It was a business trip, of sorts. My son, JP, is into speedcubing, a hobby where people compete to solve a Rubik’s Cube as fast as possible. He can solve a traditional 3-by-3 cube in less than 12 seconds. Amazing, right? Until you meet kids who can solve it in under 5 seconds.
 JP started this hobby less than two years ago, and now he’s regularly in the final rounds of these events. He grinds hard on this hobby, and it shows. I consider myself the official chauffeur, private chef and videographer of Team JP. Maybe one day he’ll let me coach him, but he isn’t ready to admit I have any good ideas.
 Occasionally my son tries to convince me to learn how to solve a cube. “It’s easy,” he insists.
 I always stop him. I think back to the terrifying few weeks he was in the neonatal intensive care unit following a serious brain injury during delivery. The doctors couldn’t predict how things would go for him. They couldn’t tell me whether he would walk or talk on schedule, much less whether he’d be into an intense mind-sport like cubing. His future hung in the balance for what seemed like eternity.
 “To me, watching you solve a cube the way you do is like magic,” I always tell him. “I don’t know how you do it. I don’t want to know how you do it. If I knew how, then it wouldn’t be magic anymore. And I don’t want that.”
 He shrugs, not really understanding, and instead decides to bug his mother about it.
 His mother, Trina, takes the end of summer hard. She’s a sad critter when the weather gets colder. Because she works in an office, she has even less daylight to enjoy.
 We spent the Friday before daylight saving time ended on a boat tour of the Savannah River, trying to avoid sunburn as we sat on the top deck of the Georgia Queen. My little family has diverse interests, but we are all fascinated by the flow of boat traffic on the Savannah River. How do boats stacked high with cargo containers float weightlessly through this narrow neck of water? Why is this tiny, barely changing corner of the South so critical to the global economy? It must be magic.
 The trip back from Savannah passed quickly and quietly. We were an hour richer in sleep but still exhausted. My family was preoccupied with technology. I was listening to my playlist, thinking about the logistics of getting my walk in before sunset. That’s always a game I have to play now that the sun sets by 6 p.m. Driving home from work feels like meeting a deadline.
 Keeping the seasonal blues at bay can be a chore, but my wife has started a new household tradition. Every year, in late December, our family marks the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year. We turn out all the lights and reflect on the darkness. Then we slowly light the candles to celebrate the imminent return of the light. We read “The Shortest Day,” a poem by Susan Cooper.
 “They carol, feast, give thanks, / And dearly love their friends, / And hope for peace.”
 Solistice candles and a copy of “The Shortest Day.”
 DAN WHISENHUNT/APPEN MEDIA 
 My wife told me she started the solstice tradition because someone once reminded her that as we become adults and the allure of Christmas wanes, we have to make our own magic to fill the void.
 And indeed, every solstice observance is like casting a ritual spell to banish the darkness from our midst for good. Seeing our candlelit faces in the darkness every year is a moment of magic that I’d prolong forever if I could.
 But the candles go out and the lights come on. And we move forward, together.
